The assassination of Egyptian President Anwar Sadat. Cairo. 1981

Anwar Sadat, the President of Egypt, was assassinated during the annual victory parade held in Cairo to celebrate the 1973 Operation Badr, during which the Egyptian Army had crossed the Suez Canal and taken back a small part of the Sinai Peninsula from Israel at the beginning of the Yom Kippur War. Following the Camp David Accords in 1978, Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize. Egypt's Islamists felt betrayed by the Accord and publicly called for the overthrow of the Egyptian president and the replacement of the nation's system of government with a government based on Islamic theocracy.

In the review stands, Sadat was protected by four layers of security and eight bodyguards, and the army parade should have been safe due to ammunition-seizure rules. As Egyptian Air Force Mirage jets flew overhead, Egyptian Army soldiers and troop trucks towing artillery paraded by. One truck contained the assassination squad. As it passed the tribune, the driver was forced to stop at gunpoint. The assassins dismounted and threw three grenades at Sadat, only one of which exploded and began indiscriminately firing AK-47 assault rifles into the stands until they had exhausted their ammunition and then attempted to flee.

Sadat and ten others were killed and 28 were wounded. One of the attackers was killed, and the three others injured and arrested. then tried, found guilty and executed by firing squad in April 1982.
